clue: Honors the birthday of a Belgian inventor whose brass instrument is played with a reed
description: Celebrates the saxophone on the birthday of its inventor, Adolphe Sax, born in Dinant, Belgium, on November 6, 1814.
fact: Although it is made of brass, the saxophone is classed as a woodwind because its sound comes from a reed.

clue: Born in Warsaw in 1867, she discovered polonium and radium
description: The physicist and chemist who pioneered research on radioactivity was born in Warsaw on November 7, 1867.
fact: She is still the only person to win Nobel Prizes in two different sciences: physics in 1903 and chemistry in 1911.

clue: Hindus light oil lamps and fireworks to honor the triumph of light over darkness
description: The Hindu festival of lights celebrates the victory of good over evil. In 2026 its main day, Lakshmi Puja on the new moon of Kartik, falls on November 8.
fact: The name comes from the Sanskrit 'deepavali', meaning 'a row of lamps'.

clue: In 1989 jubilant crowds climbed and chipped at a barrier that had split a city since 1961
description: On the night of November 9, 1989, East German border crossings opened and crowds poured through, a big step toward German reunification.
fact: The opening was partly an accident: an official wrongly announced at a press conference that new travel rules applied immediately.

clue: Big Bird, Elmo and Cookie Monster first appeared on TV in 1969
description: The children's TV show premiered on American public television on November 10, 1969, mixing puppets, songs and early learning.
fact: The show has been adapted into many local versions, from Mexico's Plaza Sésamo to Germany's Sesamstraße.

clue: The date 11.11 looks like four lone figures, so China turned it into a shopping spree
description: Started by Chinese students in the 1990s as a day for people without partners, 11/11 has become the world's biggest online shopping event.
fact: Alibaba began promoting 11.11 sales in 2009; within a decade it was selling tens of billions of dollars of goods in a single day.

clue: In 2014 a European probe named Philae touched down on an icy body called 67P
description: On November 12, 2014, the Philae lander from ESA's Rosetta mission made the first-ever soft landing on a comet, 67P/Churyumov-Gerasimenko.
fact: Philae's anchoring harpoons failed to fire, so it bounced twice before settling in a shadowy spot far from its target.

clue: A day to hold doors, pay compliments and do good turns for strangers
description: Introduced in 1998 by the World Kindness Movement, a coalition of groups from many countries, to encourage good deeds big and small.
fact: The World Kindness Movement grew out of a 1997 conference of kindness organizations held in Tokyo.

clue: India marks Jawaharlal Nehru's birthday with school fun and treats for kids
description: India celebrates its young people on the birthday of its first prime minister, Jawaharlal Nehru, born November 14, 1889, who was fondly called 'Chacha Nehru'.
fact: 'Chacha' means 'uncle' in Hindi, a nickname reflecting Nehru's well-known affection for kids.

clue: Japanese kids aged three, five and seven visit shrines dressed in kimono
description: On November 15, Japanese families take girls aged 3 and 7 and boys aged 5 (sometimes 3) to Shinto shrines to pray for healthy growth.
fact: Children receive chitose-ame, long red-and-white 'thousand-year candy' sticks that symbolize a long life.

clue: Mexico honors the 1910 uprising against Porfirio Diaz with parades
description: Recalls the start of the Mexican Revolution on November 20, 1910. The public holiday is the third Monday of November, which in 2026 is November 16.
fact: Mexico City's Monument to the Revolution was first meant to be a grand legislative palace, left unfinished when the fighting began.

clue: Opened in 1869, this Egyptian waterway links the Mediterranean and the Red Sea
description: The canal opened on November 17, 1869, letting ships sail between Europe and Asia without going all the way around Africa.
fact: Verdi's opera Aida is often linked to the opening, but it premiered in Cairo two years later, in 1871.

clue: A Disney cartoon star with round black ears debuted in Steamboat Willie in 1928
description: Disney counts November 18, 1928, the New York premiere of the sound cartoon Steamboat Willie, as the birthday of its most famous character.
fact: Walt Disney himself voiced the character until 1947.

clue: French red wine released on the third Thursday of November, uncorked at 12:01 a.m.
description: The first wine of the harvest from France's Beaujolais region goes on sale on the third Thursday of November, which is November 19 in 2026.
fact: It is made from Gamay grapes and bottled just weeks after the harvest, so it is meant to be drunk young.

clue: Swedish author of Nils Holgersson and first woman to win the Nobel in literature
description: Born November 20, 1858, in Värmland, Sweden, she wrote The Wonderful Adventures of Nils and in 1909 became the first woman awarded the Nobel Prize in Literature.
fact: She was featured on Sweden's 20-kronor banknote, with Nils riding a goose on the back.

clue: In 1783 two men drifted over Paris beneath a Montgolfier brothers' envelope
description: On November 21, 1783, Pilâtre de Rozier and the Marquis d'Arlandes made the first free flight with people aboard, in a Montgolfier craft over Paris.
fact: Before risking humans, the Montgolfiers sent up a sheep, a duck and a rooster in September 1783.

clue: The feast of the patron of musicians, often marked with concerts and choir festivals
description: November 22 is the feast of Saint Cecilia, an early Roman Christian venerated as the patron saint of music and musicians.
fact: Henry Purcell and George Frideric Handel both wrote odes for her feast, including Handel's 1739 Ode for St. Cecilia's Day.

clue: A time-traveling alien in a blue police box first hit British TV in 1963
description: The BBC science-fiction series premiered on November 23, 1963, following a mysterious traveler through time and space.
fact: The TARDIS is bigger on the inside; its name stands for Time And Relative Dimension In Space.

clue: Sikhs mark their founder's birth with processions and free community meals
description: Sikhs celebrate the birth of Guru Nanak, founder of Sikhism, on the full moon of the month of Kartik, which falls on November 24 in 2026.
fact: Gurdwaras serve free langar meals to anyone; the Golden Temple's kitchen feeds tens of thousands of people a day.

clue: In France, unmarried women of 25 wear wild yellow-and-green hats
description: On November 25, the feast of Saint Catherine, France celebrates 'Catherinettes', unmarried women aged 25, especially in fashion houses, with extravagant homemade hats.
fact: The French phrase 'coiffer Sainte-Catherine' (to put on Saint Catherine's hat) once meant reaching 25 while still unmarried.

clue: Americans gather for turkey, pumpkin pie and football on the fourth Thursday
description: The US holiday falls on the fourth Thursday of November, November 26 in 2026, recalling a 1621 harvest feast of Plymouth colonists and the Wampanoag.
fact: Abraham Lincoln made it a national holiday in 1863; Canada celebrates its own version in October.

clue: The day after the US turkey holiday, when stores open early with deep discounts
description: The Friday after US Thanksgiving, November 27 in 2026, traditionally kicks off the Christmas shopping season with big sales.
fact: The name was popularized by Philadelphia police in the 1950s and 60s, who dreaded the traffic and crowds that day.

clue: Marks Ismail Qemali raising a red banner with a black double-headed eagle in 1912
description: Albania celebrates independence from the Ottoman Empire, declared in Vlorë on November 28, 1912, the date Skanderbeg is said to have raised the same flag in 1443.
fact: Albanians often make a double-headed eagle gesture by linking their thumbs and spreading their fingers.

clue: A boy pharaoh's treasure-packed tomb was formally opened in 1922
description: On November 29, 1922, the tomb of the young pharaoh in Egypt's Valley of the Kings was officially opened, days after Howard Carter first peered inside.
fact: Asked if he could see anything as he first looked in by candlelight, Carter reportedly answered: 'Yes, wonderful things.'

clue: Born in 1835, he created Tom Sawyer and Huckleberry Finn
description: Samuel Clemens, who wrote under this pen name, was born on November 30, 1835, in Florida, Missouri.
fact: He was born shortly after a visit of Halley's Comet and died in 1910, a day after its next closest approach to the Sun, just as he had predicted.

clue: Children open a little door each morning on the countdown to Christmas
description: On December 1, children open the first door of this countdown calendar, a custom that began among German Protestants in the 19th century.
fact: The first printed version is credited to the Munich publisher Gerhard Lang in the early 1900s.

clue: Marks the 1971 union of six emirates, with Ras Al Khaimah joining soon after
description: Celebrates the union of the emirates on December 2, 1971, with fireworks, parades and buildings lit in red, green, white and black.
fact: Ras Al Khaimah became the seventh emirate in February 1972, a couple of months after the union was declared.

clue: In 1967 surgeon Christiaan Barnard performed the first one in Cape Town
description: On December 3, 1967, at Groote Schuur Hospital in Cape Town, Christiaan Barnard's team performed the first human-to-human heart transplant.
fact: The patient, Louis Washkansky, lived 18 days; today many recipients live for decades.

clue: Jews light one more candle each night on an eight-branched menorah
description: The Jewish festival of lights recalls the rededication of the Temple in Jerusalem. In 2026 the first candle is lit at sundown on Friday, December 4.
fact: Foods fried in oil, like latkes and sufganiyot doughnuts, recall the legend of one day's oil burning for eight days.

clue: On Dutch 'gift evening', a bearded bishop from Spain leaves presents and poems
description: On the evening of December 5, Dutch families celebrate Pakjesavond, exchanging gifts and teasing poems in the name of Saint Nicholas.
fact: Dutch settlers in New York helped bring the figure to America, where he evolved into Santa Claus.

clue: Finns light two candles in their windows to mark breaking away from Russia in 1917
description: Finland declared independence from Russia on December 6, 1917. The day is marked with candles, a presidential ball and a calm, patriotic mood.
fact: The televised presidential reception, where hundreds of guests shake the president's hand, is one of Finland's most-watched broadcasts every year.

clue: Apollo 17's crew snapped a famous photo of the whole, fully lit Earth in 1972
description: On December 7, 1972, astronauts aboard Apollo 17 photographed the entire sunlit Earth, creating one of the most reproduced images in history.
fact: Full-disk shots like this are rare because the Sun had to be directly behind the astronauts.

clue: Catholic feast on which Italians traditionally put up their Christmas trees
description: This Catholic feast honors the belief that Mary was conceived free of original sin; in Italy, Spain and other countries it is a public holiday.
fact: In Rome, the pope traditionally visits the Marian column near the Spanish Steps on this day to pray and lay flowers.

clue: Douglas Engelbart showed off a wooden pointing device in a famous 1968 demo
description: On December 9, 1968, Douglas Engelbart demonstrated the device, plus hypertext and video calls, in San Francisco in what became known as 'The Mother of All Demos'.
fact: The first prototype was a carved wooden block with two metal wheels underneath.

clue: Laureates get medals in Stockholm and Oslo on the anniversary of Alfred's death
description: The prizes are presented on December 10, the anniversary of Alfred Nobel's death in 1896: in Stockholm for most categories and in Oslo for peace.
fact: The menu of the Stockholm banquet, including the dessert, is kept secret until the night itself.

clue: Argentina honors Carlos Gardel and Julio De Caro, both born on this date
description: Buenos Aires celebrates its signature dance and music on December 11, the shared birthday of singer Carlos Gardel and bandleader Julio De Caro.
fact: UNESCO added the dance to its Intangible Cultural Heritage list in 2009, after a joint bid by Argentina and Uruguay.

clue: Millions of pilgrims visit a Mexico City basilica honoring a 1531 vision of Mary
description: Mexico's most important religious feast celebrates the apparitions of the Virgin Mary to Juan Diego on the hill of Tepeyac in 1531.
fact: The basilica in Mexico City is one of the most visited Catholic shrines in the world, drawing millions of pilgrims around December 12.

clue: A girl in white with a crown of candles leads a singing procession in Sweden
description: Swedes mark the feast of Saint Lucy on December 13 with candlelit processions, songs and saffron buns, bringing light to the darkest time of year.
fact: Under the old Julian calendar, December 13 fell close to the winter solstice, the longest night of the year.

clue: In 1911 Roald Amundsen's Norwegian team got there first, beating Scott
description: On December 14, 1911, Roald Amundsen and four companions became the first people to reach it, about five weeks before Robert Falcon Scott's team.
fact: Amundsen left a tent with a letter for Scott, asking him to deliver it to Norway's king in case the Norwegians did not make it home.

clue: Fans of Zamenhof's invented international language gather on his birthday
description: Speakers of the constructed language celebrate December 15, the birthday of its creator L. L. Zamenhof, born in 1859 in Białystok, now in Poland.
fact: Zamenhof published it in 1887 under the pen name 'Doktoro Esperanto', meaning 'Doctor Hopeful'.

clue: German composer of the Fifth Symphony and Ode to Joy, baptized in Bonn in 1770
description: The composer was baptized in Bonn on December 17, 1770; his birthday is traditionally celebrated on December 16.
fact: He kept composing after going almost completely deaf, including his famous Ninth Symphony.

clue: In 1903 Orville flew for 12 seconds over the dunes of Kitty Hawk
description: On December 17, 1903, near Kitty Hawk, North Carolina, Orville and Wilbur made the first controlled, powered airplane flights.
fact: A scrap of the 1903 Flyer's fabric traveled to Mars aboard NASA's Ingenuity helicopter in 2021.

clue: Commemorates Sheikh Jassim bin Mohammed taking power in 1878
description: Qatar celebrates the 1878 succession of Sheikh Jassim bin Mohammed Al Thani, regarded as the founder of the state, with parades and fireworks in Doha.
fact: The 2022 FIFA World Cup final in Lusail was played on December 18, this very holiday.

clue: Dickens's 1843 tale of the miser Scrooge and three ghosts
description: Charles Dickens's novella about Ebenezer Scrooge was published on December 19, 1843, and its first printing sold out by Christmas Eve.
fact: Dickens wrote it in about six weeks, partly to pay off his debts.

clue: Frank Capra's 1946 tale of George Bailey and a guardian angel named Clarence
description: Frank Capra's holiday classic starring James Stewart premiered in New York on December 20, 1946.
fact: It disappointed at the box office and became a holiday staple only after its copyright lapsed and TV stations aired it freely.

clue: The longest night in the north, when the Sun sits lowest in the sky at noon
description: In 2026 the December solstice falls on December 21, giving the Northern Hemisphere its shortest day and the Southern Hemisphere its longest.
fact: Iranians celebrate Yalda Night around the solstice, staying up late with pomegranates, watermelon and poetry by Hafez.

clue: Chinese families mark the shortest day with dumplings or sweet tangyuan rice balls
description: The Chinese winter festival falls on December 22 in 2026. Families reunite to eat dumplings in the north and glutinous rice balls in the south.
fact: A northern Chinese saying warns that if you skip dumplings on this day, your ears will freeze off.

clue: In Oaxaca, artists carve giant root vegetables into nativity scenes and figures
description: Every December 23, Oaxaca, Mexico, holds a contest of elaborate scenes carved from oversized radishes, a tradition dating to 1897.
fact: The carvings start wilting within hours, so they can only be displayed for a single evening.

clue: Many Europeans open presents tonight; elsewhere children hang up stockings
description: The evening before Christmas Day is the main celebration in much of Europe and Latin America, with festive dinners, midnight Mass and gifts.
fact: In Iceland many families give books on this evening and spend the night reading, a custom called Jólabókaflóð.

clue: Christians celebrate the birth of Jesus with carols, decorated trees and gifts
description: On December 25, Christians and many others celebrate the Nativity with church services, family meals and presents.
fact: An 1848 picture of Queen Victoria and Prince Albert around a decorated tree helped make the German custom popular in Britain and America.

clue: British holiday after Christmas, named for gifts once given to servants
description: A public holiday in the UK and many Commonwealth countries, now known for football fixtures, horse racing and big sales.
fact: Its name likely comes from 'Christmas boxes' of money or gifts given to servants and tradespeople.

clue: German astronomer who showed that planets travel in elliptical orbits
description: Born December 27, 1571, in Weil der Stadt, Germany, he worked out the three laws of planetary motion.
fact: He also wrote Somnium, a tale of a journey to the Moon often called one of the first works of science fiction.

clue: In 1895 Auguste and Louis held the first paid film screening at a Paris cafe
description: On December 28, 1895, at the Grand Café in Paris, they projected ten short films to a paying audience, often seen as the birth of cinema.
fact: Fittingly, their surname means 'light' in French.

clue: A seven-day African American celebration with a candle holder called a kinara
description: Created in 1966 by Maulana Karenga, the festival runs from December 26 to January 1, honoring African heritage with one principle for each day.
fact: Its name comes from the Swahili phrase 'matunda ya kwanza', meaning 'first fruits'.

clue: Born in Bombay in 1865, he wrote The Jungle Book and the Just So Stories
description: The author was born in Bombay (now Mumbai) on December 30, 1865, and in 1907 became the youngest-ever winner of the Nobel Prize in Literature.
fact: He invented the name Mowgli; in the stories it is said to mean 'little frog'.

clue: Midnight countdowns, fireworks and a kiss as the calendar flips over
description: The last night of the year is celebrated worldwide, with midnight fireworks rolling across time zones from Kiribati to American Samoa.
fact: In Spain, people eat 12 grapes at midnight, one on each chime of the clock, for luck in each month ahead.

clue: The Vienna Philharmonic plays Strauss waltzes for a global TV audience
description: Every January 1 the Vienna Philharmonic performs in the Golden Hall of the Musikverein; the broadcast is seen in over 90 countries.
fact: The encore always ends with the Radetzky March, with the audience clapping along under the conductor's direction.

clue: The Foundation author who came up with the Three Laws of Robotics
description: The science-fiction writer, born in Russia around 1920, celebrated his birthday on January 2. He wrote or edited more than 500 books.
fact: He coined the word 'robotics' in a 1941 short story.

clue: Fans raise a glass at 9 p.m. to The Hobbit's author, born this day in 1892
description: Each January 3, the Tolkien Society asks fans worldwide to stand at 9 p.m. local time, raise a glass and toast 'The Professor' on his birthday.
fact: J.R.R. Tolkien was born in Bloemfontein, South Africa, in 1892 and moved to England as a small child.

clue: Raised dots let blind people read; their French inventor was born in 1809
description: The UN marks January 4, the birthday of Louis Braille, born in France in 1809, to promote the reading system used by blind and partially sighted people.
fact: He was just 15 when he developed his system, adapting a military code for reading in the dark.

clue: A city in northeast China fills with glowing castles carved from frozen river blocks
description: The Harbin International Ice and Snow Sculpture Festival officially opens on January 5 each year, though its sites often welcome visitors earlier.
fact: Much of the building material is cut straight from the frozen Songhua River.

clue: Spanish children get gifts from Melchior, Caspar and Balthazar
description: Epiphany on January 6 recalls the Magi visiting the baby Jesus. In Spain and Latin America it is a gift-giving day, after parades the evening before.
fact: Spaniards eat roscón de reyes, a ring cake hiding a small figurine and a dried bean.

clue: Called Genna, it follows the old Julian calendar and a 43-day fast
description: Ethiopian Orthodox Christians, like several other Orthodox churches, celebrate the Nativity on January 7, often with all-night services in white clothing.
fact: Genna shares its name with a hockey-like game traditionally played with curved sticks on this holiday.

clue: The King of Rock and Roll, born in Tupelo, Mississippi, in 1935
description: Born January 8, 1935; fans gather at Graceland, his home in Memphis, every year on his birthday.
fact: He almost never performed outside the US; his only foreign concerts were three shows in Canada in 1957.

clue: Steve Jobs unveiled Apple's touchscreen handset in San Francisco in 2007
description: Steve Jobs introduced it at Macworld on January 9, 2007; it went on sale in the US that June.
fact: Apple's product photos traditionally show the time 9:41, roughly when Jobs revealed it during his keynote.

clue: The world's first subway opened in 1863 between Paddington and Farringdon
description: The Metropolitan Railway opened on January 10, 1863, the world's first underground railway, running steam trains through tunnels.
fact: Despite the name, more than half of the network actually runs above ground.

clue: Young Japanese adults dress up in kimono for ceremonies on the second Monday of January
description: Held on the second Monday of January, January 11 in 2027, it honors young adults with town-hall ceremonies, festive kimono and parties.
fact: Japan lowered its legal adult age to 18 in 2022, but most ceremonies still invite those turning 20.

clue: Holy premiere! The caped crusader's campy TV series began in 1966
description: The colorful ABC series starring Adam West premiered on January 12, 1966, with comic-book sound effects like 'POW!' flashing on screen.
fact: It aired twice a week: a Wednesday cliffhanger was resolved on Thursday.

clue: Punjabis dance around bonfires and toss in popcorn and sesame sweets
description: This Punjabi winter festival is held the night before Makar Sankranti, on January 13 in 2027, marking the end of winter and the sugarcane harvest.
fact: It is celebrated with extra fanfare by families marking a newborn's or a newly married couple's first one.

clue: Russians toast the old Julian calendar's January 1 with a second round of festivities
description: Many people in Russia and other former Soviet countries celebrate again on the night of January 13–14, which is January 1 under the Julian calendar.
fact: Russia switched to the Gregorian calendar only in 1918, after the revolution.

clue: Tamils boil rice with milk and jaggery until the pot spills over for good luck
description: The Tamil harvest festival gives thanks to the sun; its main day, Thai Pongal, falls on January 15 in 2027.
fact: The sweet rice dish shares the festival's name, which means 'boiling over' in Tamil.

clue: Cervantes's deluded knight first tilted at windmills in a 1605 book
description: The first part of Miguel de Cervantes's novel was published in Madrid in January 1605, traditionally dated to January 16.
fact: It is often called the first modern novel and is one of the best-selling books ever written.

clue: On Saint Anthony's feast, Spanish priests sprinkle holy water on pets and livestock
description: On January 17, the feast of Saint Anthony the Abbot, patron of animals, owners bring pets and farm animals to churches across Spain to be blessed.
fact: On Mallorca the eve of the feast is celebrated with bonfires and dancing devils.

clue: Honors the civil rights leader who gave the 'I Have a Dream' speech
description: The US federal holiday falls on the third Monday of January, January 18 in 2027, near Dr. King's birthday on January 15, 1929.
fact: At 35, he was the youngest man to receive the Nobel Peace Prize when he won it in 1964.

clue: Author of The Raven, born in Boston in 1809, master of the macabre tale
description: Born January 19, 1809, he is credited with inventing the detective story with The Murders in the Rue Morgue.
fact: Baltimore's NFL team, the Ravens, is named after his most famous poem.

clue: San Sebastian drums nonstop for 24 hours, starting at midnight on its patron's day
description: On January 20, the feast of Saint Sebastian, the Basque city of Donostia-San Sebastián celebrates with costumed drum companies parading for 24 hours.
fact: Many companies dress as cooks and soldiers, with the cooks beating on wooden barrels.

clue: In 1976 the supersonic airliner began passenger service from London and Paris
description: On January 21, 1976, British Airways and Air France simultaneously started the first scheduled supersonic passenger flights.
fact: It crossed the Atlantic in about three and a half hours, and its body stretched several inches from the heat of flight.

clue: Devotees of Lord Murugan climb 272 steps to Malaysia's Batu Caves
description: This Tamil Hindu festival on the full moon of the month of Thai falls on January 22 in 2027; huge crowds gather at Batu Caves near Kuala Lumpur.
fact: Many devotees carry ornate kavadi frames, and some pierce their skin with hooks and skewers as acts of devotion.

clue: French painter of Olympia and A Bar at the Folies-Bergere, born in 1832
description: Born in Paris on January 23, 1832, he painted scandalous modern scenes that bridged realism and impressionism.
fact: His Luncheon on the Grass was rejected by the official Paris Salon of 1863 and shown instead at the Salon des Refusés.

clue: In La Paz, people buy tiny houses, cars and banknotes hoping to get the real thing
description: The fair opens in La Paz, Bolivia, every January 24, honoring Ekeko, the Andean god of abundance; the miniatures are blessed at noon.
fact: UNESCO added the festival to its Intangible Cultural Heritage list in 2017.

clue: Scots address a haggis and recite poems by their national bard
description: Scots honor the poet Robert Burns, born January 25, 1759, with a supper of haggis, whisky and readings of his verse.
fact: 'Auld Lang Syne', sung worldwide on New Year's Eve, is a song he wrote down and adapted.

clue: Marks the 1788 arrival of the First Fleet at Sydney Cove
description: Australia's national day recalls the British First Fleet's arrival in 1788; it is a public holiday with barbecues, awards and fireworks.
fact: Thousands of people become Australian citizens at ceremonies held across the country on this day.

clue: Salzburg-born child prodigy who wrote The Magic Flute, born in 1756
description: Born in Salzburg on January 27, 1756, he wrote more than 600 works in a life of just 35 years.
fact: His baptismal name included Theophilus, which he later rendered in Latin as Amadeus, 'loved by God'.

clue: A Danish toy company patented its stud-and-tube plastic building block in 1958
description: On January 28, 1958, the Danish company filed the patent for its interlocking plastic brick, the design still used today.
fact: The company name comes from the Danish 'leg godt', meaning 'play well'.

clue: Karl Benz filed a patent for his three-wheeled motor carriage in 1886
description: On January 29, 1886, Karl Benz applied for a patent for his gasoline-powered vehicle, often called the birth certificate of the modern car.
fact: In 1888 his wife Bertha drove it about 106 km to her mother's house, the first long-distance car trip.

clue: The Beatles' last public performance, atop Apple's London office in 1969
description: On January 30, 1969, the Beatles played a surprise 42-minute set on top of 3 Savile Row until police asked them to stop.
fact: John Lennon closed it by saying: 'I hope we've passed the audition.'

clue: Viennese composer of the Unfinished Symphony and over 600 songs, born in 1797
description: Born in Vienna on January 31, 1797, he wrote more than 600 songs before his death at just 31.
fact: His friends held informal evenings devoted to his music, called Schubertiades.

clue: The Irish weave rush crosses on the first day of spring and get a bank holiday
description: Ireland honors its female patron saint on February 1, the old Celtic start of spring (Imbolc). Since 2023 it has a public holiday, on February 1 in 2027.
fact: It was the first Irish public holiday named after a woman.

clue: If Punxsutawney Phil sees his shadow, expect six more weeks of winter
description: In Punxsutawney, Pennsylvania, crowds watch a famous rodent on February 2 to 'forecast' whether spring will come early.
fact: The custom comes from German immigrants, who watched badgers on Candlemas.

clue: Japanese families throw roasted soybeans, shouting 'demons out, luck in'
description: Held the day before the traditional start of spring, February 3 in 2027, it chases away evil with bean-throwing at homes, shrines and temples.
fact: Many people eat a long uncut sushi roll, ehomaki, in silence while facing the year's lucky direction.

clue: Poles devour rose-jam paczki doughnuts on the last Thursday before Lent
description: Poland's Tłusty Czwartek is the last Thursday before Lent, February 4 in 2027, when people eat millions of filled doughnuts.
fact: In the German Rhineland the same day is Weiberfastnacht, when women playfully snip off men's ties.

clue: Giant sculptures and ice slides fill Odori Park in Hokkaido's capital
description: Japan's famous winter festival runs February 4–11, 2027, in Sapporo, with enormous sculptures across three sites.
fact: It began in 1950, when local high school students built six statues in Odori Park.

clue: Red lanterns, dumplings and firecrackers welcome the Fire Goat
description: The Chinese calendar's new year begins on February 6, 2027, with the new moon, starting the Year of the Goat.
fact: The holiday triggers the world's largest annual human migration, as hundreds of millions travel home.

clue: Samba schools parade with giant floats through the Sambadrome
description: Brazil's most famous party fills the days before Lent; Carnival Sunday, February 7 in 2027, is one of the main nights of samba-school parades.
fact: The Sambadrome was designed by architect Oscar Niemeyer and opened in 1984.

clue: Cologne and Dusseldorf throw tons of candy from carnival floats
description: The highlight of Rhineland carnival falls two days before Ash Wednesday, February 8 in 2027, with huge parades in Cologne, Düsseldorf and Mainz.
fact: The German name Rosenmontag probably comes from a dialect word for romping about, not from the flower.

clue: A Shrove Tuesday treat; in Olney women race while flipping one in a pan
description: On Shrove Tuesday, February 9 in 2027, Britons use up eggs and butter before Lent, topping thin batter cakes with lemon and sugar.
fact: The Olney Pancake Race in Buckinghamshire is said to have been run since 1445.

clue: Christians receive a cross of grey dust on the forehead to start Lent
description: The first day of Lent falls 46 days before Easter; in 2027 that is February 10.
fact: The ashes are often made by burning palm branches from the previous year's Palm Sunday.

clue: In 1990 South Africa's most famous prisoner walked free after 27 years
description: On February 11, 1990, Nelson Mandela left Victor Verster Prison, a turning point toward the end of apartheid and his election as president in 1994.
fact: He later shared the 1993 Nobel Peace Prize with F. W. de Klerk, the president who freed him.

clue: Celebrates the naturalist behind On the Origin of Species, born in 1809
description: Science fans worldwide celebrate the birthday of Charles Darwin, born February 12, 1809, the very same day as Abraham Lincoln.
fact: His voyage on HMS Beagle was planned for two years but lasted almost five.

clue: UNESCO's day for broadcasting, on the anniversary of the UN's own station from 1946
description: Proclaimed by UNESCO, February 13 marks the anniversary of the launch of United Nations Radio in 1946.
fact: Radio still reaches more people worldwide than any other medium, according to UNESCO.

clue: Cards, red roses and chocolates for sweethearts
description: Lovers exchange cards and gifts on February 14, the feast of an early Christian saint.
fact: In 2027 the Super Bowl is scheduled on this date for the first time, at SoFi Stadium in California.

clue: Pisa-born scientist who spotted Jupiter's moons through a telescope, born in 1564
description: The father of modern observational astronomy was born in Pisa on February 15, 1564.
fact: One of his fingers is on display at the Museo Galileo in Florence.

clue: A DuPont chemist's 1937 patent for a silky synthetic fiber, later famous in stockings
description: On February 16, 1937, Wallace Carothers of DuPont was granted the patent behind the first fully synthetic fiber.
fact: When stockings made from it went on sale in 1940, millions of pairs sold within days.

clue: Puccini's opera about a Nagasaki geisha flopped at La Scala in 1904
description: Puccini's opera premiered at La Scala, Milan, on February 17, 1904, and was booed; a revised version months later was a triumph.
fact: It is now one of the most frequently performed operas in the world.

clue: Clyde Tombaugh spotted this distant world at Lowell Observatory in 1930
description: On February 18, 1930, Clyde Tombaugh found it by comparing photographic plates; it was reclassified as a dwarf planet in 2006.
fact: Its name was suggested by Venetia Burney, an 11-year-old schoolgirl in Oxford.

clue: Torun-born astronomer who put the Sun, not Earth, at the center, born in 1473
description: Born on February 19, 1473, in Toruń, Poland, he argued that Earth and the planets orbit the Sun.
fact: Legend says he received the first printed copy of his great book on his deathbed in 1543.

clue: On the year's first full moon, people solve riddles and eat sweet tangyuan
description: Falling on the 15th day of the first lunar month, February 20 in 2027, it closes the New Year season with glowing displays.
fact: Riddles are traditionally attached to the lanterns for visitors to guess.

clue: In 1804 Richard Trevithick's engine hauled iron and passengers in Wales
description: On February 21, 1804, Trevithick's engine pulled a train along the Penydarren tramway in Wales, the first railway journey by a steam locomotive.
fact: It hauled 10 tons of iron, five wagons and about 70 men on a trip of nearly ten miles.

clue: Japan picked 2/22 because 'ni ni ni' sounds like a meow
description: Japan's Neko no Hi, chosen by a vote of cat lovers, falls on February 22 because 'ni' (two) echoes 'nyan', the Japanese 'meow'.
fact: Japan has many cafes devoted to the animals and several islands where they outnumber people.

clue: Composer of Messiah and Water Music, born in Halle in 1685
description: Born February 23, 1685, in Halle, Germany, he settled in London and became a British subject.
fact: Audiences traditionally stand for the Hallelujah chorus, a custom said to go back to King George II.

clue: A 1582 papal bull fixed the drifting date of Easter by skipping ten days
description: On February 24, 1582, Pope Gregory XIII issued the bull Inter gravissimas, creating the calendar most of the world uses today.
fact: To catch up, Catholic countries jumped straight from October 4 to October 15, 1582.

clue: Honors the 1950 accession of Emir Abdullah Al-Salem Al-Sabah
description: Kuwait celebrates on February 25 with fireworks and parades, honoring Sheikh Abdullah Al-Salem, who led the country to independence in 1961.
fact: Liberation Day follows the next day, giving the country a back-to-back festive holiday.

clue: French author of Les Miserables and The Hunchback of Notre-Dame, born in 1802
description: Born in Besançon on February 26, 1802, he was a towering figure of French Romanticism.
fact: About two million people are said to have joined his funeral procession in Paris in 1885.

clue: Marks the 1844 break from Haiti, with carnival parades in Santo Domingo
description: The Dominican Republic declared independence on February 27, 1844; the day also caps the country's carnival season.
fact: Its flag is one of the very few national flags to show an image of the Bible.

clue: Finland honors its national epic, compiled by Elias Lonnrot in 1835
description: On February 28, Finland celebrates the date Elias Lönnrot signed the preface to the first edition in 1835; it is also Finnish Culture Day.
fact: Its tales helped inspire J.R.R. Tolkien, who tried to learn Finnish to read it in the original.

clue: The Welsh wear daffodils and leeks to honor their patron saint
description: Wales celebrates its patron saint on March 1, traditionally the date of his death in 589, with parades, Welsh cakes and national dress.
fact: His last sermon reportedly urged: 'Do the little things.'

clue: Author of The Cat in the Hat and Green Eggs and Ham, born in 1904
description: Theodor Geisel was born on March 2, 1904; his birthday anchors Read Across America events in US schools.
fact: Green Eggs and Ham uses just 50 different words, the result of a bet with his publisher.

clue: Japanese families display tiers of dolls in imperial court robes for their daughters
description: On March 3, Japanese families with girls display ornamental dolls and enjoy diamond-shaped rice cakes and chirashi sushi.
fact: Many families pack the dolls away quickly afterwards; folklore says leaving them out delays a daughter's marriage.

clue: Venetian violinist-priest who wrote The Four Seasons, born in 1678
description: Born in Venice on March 4, 1678, he composed hundreds of concertos and dozens of operas.
fact: Because of his hair he was nicknamed 'il Prete Rosso', the Red Priest.

clue: Flemish mapmaker whose 1569 projection makes Greenland look gigantic
description: Born March 5, 1512, in Rupelmonde, Flanders, he created the map projection still used by many web maps today.
fact: He also popularized the word 'atlas' for a bound collection of maps.

clue: In 1957 Kwame Nkrumah declared the Gold Coast free from British rule
description: On March 6, 1957, Ghana became the first sub-Saharan African colony to gain independence.
fact: The black star on its flag became a symbol of African freedom; its national football team is nicknamed the Black Stars.

clue: A 90 km cross-country ski race from Salen to Mora in Sweden
description: The world's oldest and biggest cross-country ski race is held on the first Sunday of March, March 7 in 2027, retracing Gustav Vasa's 1520 flight.
fact: Skiers are served warm blueberry soup at refreshment stations along the course.

clue: Marked with mimosa flowers in Italy and a public holiday in many countries
description: International Women's Day on March 8 celebrates women's achievements and campaigns for equality; it is a public holiday in many countries.
fact: The date took hold after women in Petrograd went on strike on March 8, 1917, helping spark the Russian Revolution.

clue: Ruth Handler's fashion doll debuted at New York's Toy Fair in 1959
description: Mattel introduced the doll at the American International Toy Fair on March 9, 1959, now treated as her official birthday.
fact: Her full name is Barbara Millicent Roberts, after Ruth Handler's daughter Barbara.

clue: Nintendo's plumber gets a day because MAR10 looks like his name
description: Nintendo celebrates its mascot on March 10, since 'MAR10' resembles his name, with game sales and events.
fact: He first appeared in 1981's Donkey Kong as 'Jumpman', a carpenter rather than a plumber.

clue: Lesotho honors the founder of the Basotho nation with games and feasts
description: Lesotho marks March 11 in honor of King Moshoeshoe I, who united the Basotho people in the 19th century and founded the mountain kingdom.
fact: Lesotho is entirely surrounded by South Africa, and its lowest point is about 1,400 metres above sea level.

clue: Tim Berners-Lee's 1989 CERN proposal, which his boss called 'vague but exciting'
description: On March 12, 1989, Tim Berners-Lee submitted 'Information Management: A Proposal' at CERN near Geneva, the founding document of the web.
fact: The first website, info.cern.ch, is still online.

clue: William Herschel spotted this tilted ice giant from his garden in Bath in 1781
description: On March 13, 1781, William Herschel discovered it, the first planet found with a telescope.
fact: Herschel wanted to name it 'George's Star' after King George III.

clue: 3/14 is celebrated with round desserts and digit-reciting contests
description: Math fans celebrate the ratio of a circle's circumference to its diameter, roughly 3.14, on March 14.
fact: Albert Einstein was born on this date in 1879, and in 2027 the Oscars are also held on it.

clue: Budapest marks the 1848 uprising with cockades in red, white and green
description: Hungary commemorates the revolution that began on March 15, 1848, when young radicals read out the 12 Points and the National Song in Pest.
fact: People wear a small cockade in the national colors pinned to their coats.

clue: In 1926 Robert Goddard's launch in Massachusetts climbed just 12 meters
description: On March 16, 1926, in Auburn, Massachusetts, Robert Goddard launched the first liquid-fueled rocket, which flew for about 2.5 seconds.
fact: In 1920 The New York Times mocked his ideas on spaceflight; it printed a correction in 1969 as Apollo 11 headed to the Moon.

clue: Ireland's patron saint, shamrocks and a green-dyed river in Chicago
description: March 17 honors the patron saint of Ireland, with parades and celebrations around the world.
fact: Chicago has dyed its river green every year since 1962.

clue: Alexei Leonov floated outside Voskhod 2 for 12 minutes in 1965
description: On March 18, 1965, Soviet cosmonaut Alexei Leonov became the first person to leave a spacecraft in open space.
fact: His suit ballooned so much that he had to let out air to squeeze back into the airlock.

clue: Valencia burns giant satirical statues on Saint Joseph's night
description: Valencia's festival climaxes on March 19, Saint Joseph's Day, with the Cremà, when hundreds of papier-mâché sculptures go up in flames.
fact: Each year one figure, the 'ninot indultat', is saved from the flames by public vote.

clue: Day and night are nearly equal as the Sun crosses the celestial equator
description: In 2027 the March equinox falls on March 20, marking the start of astronomical spring in the north and autumn in the south.
fact: At Chichen Itza in Mexico, the sun at this time casts a serpent-shaped shadow down the pyramid steps.

clue: The Persian new year, with a table of seven symbolic items starting with S
description: Celebrated by about 300 million people from Iran to Central Asia, the Persian New Year begins at the equinox; in Iran it is March 21 in 2027.
fact: The haft-sin table holds seven items whose Persian names start with 's', such as sabzeh sprouts and serkeh vinegar.

clue: Hindus throw colored powder and water to welcome spring
description: The Hindu festival of colors follows the full moon of Phalguna; in 2027 the Holika bonfires burn on March 21 and the color play is on March 22.
fact: The bonfires the night before recall the legend of the demoness Holika.

clue: Jews read the Book of Esther, wear costumes and eat triangular hamantaschen
description: This joyful Jewish holiday recalls how Queen Esther saved the Jews of Persia; in 2027 it begins at sundown on March 22 and is celebrated on March 23.
fact: Noisemakers called graggers are spun to drown out the villain Haman's name when the story is read.

clue: Budapest-born escape artist who wriggled out of handcuffs and water tanks
description: Born Erik Weisz in Budapest on March 24, 1874, he moved to America and became the world's most famous escape artist.
fact: He spent his later years exposing fake spiritualist mediums.

clue: Celebrates the 1821 revolt against Ottoman rule with school parades in blue and white
description: Greece marks the start of its War of Independence in 1821 on March 25, which is also the Orthodox feast of the Annunciation.
fact: Greeks traditionally eat fried salt cod with garlic sauce, bakaliaros skordalia, on this day.

clue: Christians recall the crucifixion of Jesus two days before Easter
description: Commemorating the crucifixion of Jesus, it falls two days before Easter, on March 26 in 2027.
fact: In Bermuda people fly colorful kites on this day, said to symbolize Christ's ascension.

clue: Each year a famous playwright or actor writes a message read on stages worldwide
description: Created by the International Theatre Institute and first celebrated on March 27, 1962, it promotes theater in all its forms.
fact: The very first international message was written by the French artist Jean Cocteau.

clue: Chocolate eggs and bunnies mark this spring feast
description: Christians celebrate the resurrection of Jesus. In 2027 it falls on March 28, the first Sunday after the spring full moon.
fact: The date is computed from the moon, so it can land anywhere between March 22 and April 25.

clue: Poles drench each other with buckets and water pistols the day after Easter
description: On Easter Monday, March 29 in 2027, Poland celebrates Śmigus-dyngus, when friends and neighbors douse each other with water.
fact: The custom is often linked to the baptism of Poland's Duke Mieszko I on Easter in 966.

clue: Dutch painter of The Starry Night and Sunflowers, born in 1853
description: Born March 30, 1853, in Zundert, the Netherlands, he produced about 2,100 artworks in roughly a decade.
fact: He sold very few paintings during his lifetime.

clue: Gustave's iron lattice in Paris was inaugurated for the 1889 World's Fair
description: On March 31, 1889, Gustave Eiffel climbed to the top to raise the French flag at the tower's inauguration.
fact: It was meant to stand for only 20 years; its value as a radio antenna saved it from demolition.

clue: Pranks and hoaxes until noon; the French tape paper fish to people's backs
description: Around the world, people play practical jokes and newspapers publish fake stories on April 1.
fact: In 1957 the BBC aired a report on Swiss farmers harvesting spaghetti from trees.

clue: Danish author of The Little Mermaid and The Ugly Duckling, born in 1805
description: Born on April 2, 1805, in Odense, Denmark; his birthday is International Children's Book Day.
fact: Copenhagen's Little Mermaid statue, inspired by his tale, turned 100 in 2013.

clue: Motorola's Martin Cooper made the first handheld cellular call in 1973
description: On April 3, 1973, on a New York street, Martin Cooper called a rival at Bell Labs on a prototype weighing about 1 kg.
fact: The prototype's battery gave about 30 minutes of talk time and took around 10 hours to charge.

clue: Dakar marks freedom from France in 1960 with a big parade
description: Senegal's national day, April 4, recalls the 1960 agreement with France that led to independence; Dakar hosts a large parade.
fact: Senegal's first president, Léopold Sédar Senghor, was a celebrated poet and the first African member of the Académie française.

clue: Chinese families sweep ancestors' tombs, fly kites and eat green rice balls
description: Also called Tomb-Sweeping Day, it falls on April 5 in 2027, 15 days after the spring equinox.
fact: Its name means 'clear and bright', describing the fresh spring weather.

clue: Athens opened the revived Games in 1896, the dream of Pierre de Coubertin
description: On April 6, 1896, the first modern Olympic Games opened in Athens, with athletes from 14 nations.
fact: Winners received silver medals; gold medals for first place were introduced only in 1904.

clue: Revolutionary France adopted decimal units of length and mass in 1795
description: On April 7, 1795, a French law defined the metre and the gram, laying the foundation of the measurement system most of the world uses.
fact: Revolutionary France also tried decimal time, with 10-hour days, but soon gave it up.

clue: Golf's first major of the year at Augusta, where the winner gets a green jacket
description: The first round of the 2027 tournament at Augusta National Golf Club in Georgia is on April 8; the final round is on April 11.
fact: The defending champion hosts the Champions Dinner each year and chooses the menu.

clue: In 1860 a Frenchman captured a voice singing 'Au clair de la lune' as squiggles on paper
description: On April 9, 1860, Édouard-Léon Scott de Martinville's phonautograph captured part of a French folk song, the oldest known recording of a human voice.
fact: It was meant only to be seen, not heard; scientists first played it back in 2008.

clue: In 2019 astronomers revealed a glowing orange ring around the dark heart of galaxy M87
description: On April 10, 2019, the Event Horizon Telescope team released the first image of a black hole, at the center of the galaxy M87.
fact: The image combined data from radio telescopes across the globe, effectively forming an Earth-sized telescope.

clue: Oxford and Cambridge crews row the Thames from Putney to Mortlake
description: The rowing contest between Oxford and Cambridge universities, first held in 1829, takes place on April 11 in 2027.
fact: In 1877 the result was declared a dead heat, the only tie in the race's history.

clue: In 1961 the pilot of Vostok 1 became the first human in space
description: On April 12, 1961, the Soviet cosmonaut orbited Earth once in 108 minutes; fans worldwide celebrate 'Yuri's Night' on the anniversary.
fact: As he lifted off he famously said 'Poyekhali!', meaning 'Let's go!'

clue: Thailand's New Year turns into a giant nationwide water fight
description: The Thai New Year runs April 13–15, with temple visits, water gently poured over elders' hands and huge water fights in the streets.
fact: UNESCO added it to its Intangible Cultural Heritage list in 2023.

clue: Bangladesh greets the Bengali new year in red and white with colorful processions
description: The first day of the Bengali calendar falls on April 14 in Bangladesh, celebrated with music, fairs and a colorful procession in Dhaka.
fact: Dhaka's Mangal Shobhajatra procession was added to UNESCO's Intangible Cultural Heritage list in 2016.

clue: Painter of the Mona Lisa and designer of flying machines, born in 1452
description: Born April 15, 1452, near Vinci in Tuscany; his birthday is celebrated as World Art Day.
fact: He wrote many of his notes in mirror script, from right to left.

clue: London-born silent film star famous as the Little Tramp, born in 1889
description: Born in London on April 16, 1889, he became the biggest star of silent cinema.
fact: In 1919 he co-founded the United Artists studio with Mary Pickford, Douglas Fairbanks and D. W. Griffith.

clue: Celebrates Argentina's signature red wine grape, originally from France
description: Created by Wines of Argentina in 2011, April 17 recalls the date in 1853 when Argentina set out to transform its wine industry.
fact: The grape came from southwest France, but Mendoza is now its most famous home.

clue: In 1980 Rhodesia became a new nation, its capital later renamed Harare
description: Zimbabwe became independent on April 18, 1980; the anniversary is its national holiday.
fact: Bob Marley and the Wailers performed at the independence celebrations, including his song 'Zimbabwe'.

clue: The world's oldest annual 26.2-mile race, run on Patriots' Day in Massachusetts
description: Held since 1897 on Patriots' Day, the third Monday in April, which is April 19 in 2027.
fact: In 1967 Kathrine Switzer became the first woman to run it as a registered entrant, despite an official trying to stop her.

clue: Louis and Claude Bernard first heated a liquid to kill microbes in an 1862 test
description: On April 20, 1862, Louis Pasteur and Claude Bernard completed the first test of gently heating liquids to kill germs, a process now named after him.
fact: Pasteur first used it to stop wine and beer from spoiling, years before it was applied to milk.

clue: Jewish families hold a Seder with matzah to recall the Exodus from Egypt
description: The Jewish festival of freedom begins at sundown on April 21, 2027 (15 Nisan), with the Seder meal, and lasts seven or eight days.
fact: The youngest child at the Seder traditionally asks the Four Questions.

clue: Since 1970, people have planted trees and cleaned up parks for the planet on this day
description: First held on April 22, 1970, in the US, it is now marked in more than 190 countries.
fact: The first one drew an estimated 20 million Americans, about one in ten people in the country.

clue: Catalans give a rose and a book to loved ones on Saint George's Day
description: On April 23, Barcelona's streets fill with book and rose stalls for the feast of Catalonia's patron saint.
fact: UNESCO chose April 23 as World Book and Copyright Day partly inspired by this Catalan tradition.

clue: Shuttle Discovery carried this orbiting observatory aloft in 1990
description: Launched on April 24, 1990, aboard Discovery, it has made more than 1.5 million observations.
fact: Its main mirror was flawed at launch; astronauts installed corrective optics in 1993.

clue: In 1974 Lisbon soldiers toppled a dictatorship with flowers in their rifles
description: On April 25, 1974, a nearly bloodless military coup ended decades of dictatorship in Portugal; the date is now Freedom Day.
fact: A radio broadcast of the song 'Grândola, Vila Morena' was a secret signal to start the uprising.

clue: Twisted, salty knots of baked bread, said to have been invented by monks
description: National Pretzel Day on April 26 was first proclaimed in Pennsylvania in 2003 and celebrates the knotted baked snack.
fact: Legend says a monk shaped the dough to look like arms crossed in prayer.

clue: The Dutch wear orange and hold street flea markets for their monarch's birthday
description: Koningsdag on April 27 celebrates King Willem-Alexander's birthday with orange outfits, street parties and a nationwide free market.
fact: On this day almost anyone may sell second-hand goods on the street without a permit.

clue: Thor Heyerdahl's balsa raft set sail from Peru toward Polynesia in 1947
description: On April 28, 1947, Heyerdahl and five crewmates left Callao, Peru; 101 days later they reached the Tuamotu Islands.
fact: The original raft is preserved in its own museum in Oslo.

clue: Held on the birthday of ballet reformer Jean-Georges Noverre, born in 1727
description: Created in 1982 by the International Theatre Institute, a UNESCO partner, it celebrates dance of every style on April 29.
fact: Noverre's 'Letters on Dancing and Ballets' helped turn ballet into dramatic storytelling.

clue: Bonfires blaze, and legend says witches gather on the Brocken in Germany's Harz
description: On April 30, people across central and northern Europe light bonfires to welcome spring; German folklore tells of witches dancing on the Brocken.
fact: Swedes call it Valborg and sing spring songs around the fires.

clue: Mint juleps and big hats at Churchill Downs on the first Saturday of May
description: The 153rd running of the famous horse race takes place at Churchill Downs in Louisville on May 1, 2027.
fact: Nicknamed 'the most exciting two minutes in sports', the race covers about 2 km.

clue: Greeks crack red-dyed eggs and roast lamb five weeks after the Western feast
description: Orthodox churches use the Julian calendar to set the date; in 2027 their feast falls on May 2, five weeks after Western Easter.
fact: At midnight, worshippers pass the 'Holy Light' from candle to candle and greet each other with 'Christos Anesti!'

clue: Japan's string of spring holidays includes Constitution Memorial Day on May 3
description: A cluster of public holidays runs from April 29 to May 5; May 3 is Constitution Memorial Day, and millions of people travel.
fact: The name was coined by the film industry in the 1950s to lure holiday crowds into cinemas.

clue: Fans greet each other with 'May the Fourth be with you'
description: A pun on 'May the Force be with you' turned May 4 into a fan holiday for the space saga.
fact: The pun appeared in a 1979 London newspaper ad congratulating Margaret Thatcher on her election win.

clue: Commemorates Mexico's 1862 victory over French troops at Puebla
description: Marking the Battle of Puebla on May 5, 1862, it is celebrated more widely in the US than in most of Mexico.
fact: It is often mistaken for Mexico's Independence Day, which is actually September 16.

clue: In 1954 Roger Bannister broke a famous running barrier in Oxford
description: On May 6, 1954, Roger Bannister ran 3:59.4 at the Iffley Road track in Oxford, a feat many had thought impossible.
fact: His record lasted only 46 days before Australia's John Landy beat it.

clue: Russian composer of Swan Lake and The Nutcracker, born in 1840
description: Pyotr Ilyich Tchaikovsky was born on May 7, 1840, in Votkinsk, Russia.
fact: He conducted at the opening of New York's Carnegie Hall in 1891.

clue: Helston in Cornwall dances through streets and houses in its Furry Dance
description: Held on May 8 unless that is a Sunday or Monday, it fills Helston, Cornwall, with dancers in their finest clothes wearing lily of the valley.
fact: The first dance starts at 7 a.m., and the dancers weave in and out of shops and houses.

clue: Breakfast in bed and flowers for mom on the second Sunday of May
description: The US, Canada, Australia, Germany, Italy and many other countries honor mothers on the second Sunday in May, May 9 in 2027.
fact: Its founder, Anna Jarvis, later campaigned against the holiday's commercialization.

clue: East and west rail lines were joined at Promontory, Utah, in 1869 to complete a railroad
description: On May 10, 1869, the Central Pacific and Union Pacific lines joined at Promontory Summit, Utah, completing the first transcontinental railroad in the US.
fact: Wires were rigged so the hammer blows would go out by telegraph; in the end an operator simply tapped out 'DONE'.

clue: Surrealist with an upturned mustache who painted melting clocks, born in 1904
description: Born in Figueres, Catalonia, on May 11, 1904, he became the most famous Surrealist painter.
fact: He designed the Chupa Chups lollipop logo in 1969.

clue: Held on Florence Nightingale's birthday to honor those who care for patients
description: Celebrated on May 12, the birthday of Florence Nightingale, born in 1820 and regarded as the founder of modern nursing.
fact: Nightingale was also a pioneering statistician, famous for her 'rose' diagrams.

clue: The first world championship Grand Prix roared around Silverstone in 1950
description: On May 13, 1950, the first race of the new world championship was held at Silverstone, England, won by Giuseppe Farina in an Alfa Romeo.
fact: King George VI attended, the only time a reigning British monarch has watched a world championship race.

clue: Edward Jenner used cowpox to protect a boy named James Phipps in 1796
description: On May 14, 1796, Edward Jenner inoculated eight-year-old James Phipps with cowpox, the start of vaccination.
fact: The word 'vaccine' comes from the Latin 'vacca', meaning cow.

clue: Madrid's patron saint fiesta, with meadow picnics and chotis dancing
description: On May 15, Madrid honors its patron, a medieval farm laborer, with picnics by his hermitage and locals dressed as chulapos.
fact: Goya painted the crowds at the saint's meadow in his 1788 'La pradera de San Isidro'.
